The method to determine the compensation factor involved performing a best fit line to the WSTF limit points 
(black circles).

The best fit line to those points is the estimated dependence of the limiting oxygen concentration on 
forced flow velocity.

To get a conservative estimate of the slope (and thus the compensation factor) we used the one-
tailed 95 percent confidence interval.

Table 2 shows both the best fit line and the conservative estimate from the 95 
percent confidence interval.

To estimate the change in the flammability limit at 1-g  compared to lunar-g, the 
extrapolated value from the WSTF testing can be compared to the extrapolated value at lunar g.

A major limitation to 
this analysis is identification of the relevant buoyant velocity which is an area worthy of significant research.

In a 
forced-flow low-gravity experiment, the average duct velocity can be known exactly, however, due to effects such as 
boundary layer growth and thermal expansion, the velocity varies with time and location so while the average duct 
velocity is representative of the flow field, it is not necessarily the same value as the velocity at the controlling location.

For buoyant flames, with or without forced flow, the velocity at any location varies similarly to the non-buoyant case 
but it is not easily measured, particularly because the location of greatest interest is not known.

For flames on the CKL 
side, the velocity at the flame tip can be assumed to be likely the most important location but this has not been verified 
or measured accurately.

In a buoyant boundary layer, the velocity at the flame tip would not be comparable to the 
average duct velocity in non-buoyant cases.

The 1-g buoyant velocity was estimated by Takahashi16 to be 35 cm/s, 
but the lunar gravity velocity is not known.

The lunar gravity velocity has been estimated20, for spreading flames, by 
equating the buoyant boundary layer thickness with the forced flow boundary layer.

However, both of these estimates 
are difficult to verify.
Furthermore, near the extinction limit, the flame is weaker resulting in less buoyant flow.

Consequently, given the absence of a common understanding of the relevant velocity, the buoyant velocity is 
considered to be not determined in this paper.

Given this uncertainty, 35 cm/s could be considered to be a 
conservatively high estimate of the buoyant 1-g velocity.

Since the lunar velocity is also not known, extrapolating to 
zero flow would give a conservative estimate of the limit.

Extrapolating the worst-case 95% confidence interval slope 
from the data for each material (Table 2) from the presumed 1-g buoyant velocity of 35 cm/s to zero would give a 
conservative 1-g to lunar-g flammability delta that could be applied to other test methods.

These values are tabulated 
in Table 2.
The worst-case delta for these materials can be seen to be 2.3%.

The Beefy-T smoldering data are included because the NASA emphasis is on complete extinction, however since 
smoldering is a surface reaction rather than a gas-phase flame, the Damköhler number blow-off limit would not be 
expected to be applicable.
However, it is clear in figure 10 that the extinction shows similar flow dependence.

the lunar-g buoyant extinction is at substantially higher oxygen concentrations that the WSTF data.

One possible

This shift of the HTL could be attributed to 
increased radiative loss (Eq. 8) resulting from higher pyrolysis temperatures.

This mechanism was suggested by 
Takahashi16 who saw similar behavior for several high temperature materials in downward spread.

This mechanism 
merits additional study as it suggests that high temperature materials may not exhibit enhanced flammability at lunar-
temperature materials.
